Notes: Ezra 2:1-2, 21 (list of returnees with Zerubbabel, c. 538 BCE, Persian period; date c.): 'Of Bethlehem, one hundred twenty-three' among 'the people of the province' who 'returned to Jerusalem and Judah, all to their own towns'. Earliest Second Temple-period attestation of Judeans of Bethlehem. Population blank: 123 is an ancient count of returnees (men) of Bethlehem origin, a flow/subset and not a census of residents; the list's date and reliability are debated by modern scholars (e.g. Finkelstein dates its composition later). Year Established -700 (c.): earliest documented Judahite presence = First Temple-period bulla reading 'Bat Lechem' / '[Lemel]ekh' ('from Bethlehem ... to the king') found in the City of David, dated late 8th-7th c. BCE (IAA/Eli Shukron 2012; https://www.biblicalarchaeology.org/daily/earliest-history-of-bethlehem-documented-by-first-temple-period-bulla-from-the-city-of-david/), showing Bethlehem as a town of the Kingdom of Judah.

Nehemiah 7:6-7, 26 (Nehemiah's copy of the same register of returnees under Zerubbabel, c. 538 BCE; c.): 'The people of Bethlehem and Netophah, one hundred eighty-eight.' Population blank: combined figure for two towns (aggregate) and a returnee count, not residents of Bethlehem alone; it differs from Ezra 2:21-22 (123 + 56).

Encyclopaedia Judaica (Avi-Yonah, Orni et al.) via Jewish Virtual Library: 'With the return from Babylonia, the exiles from Bethlehem went back to their city' (citing Ezra 2:21; Neh. 7:26). Resettlement of Bethlehem by Judean returnees in the early Persian period (c. 538 BCE; c.). No figure for residents.

Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Beth-lehem-Judah': the only post-exilic Old Testament reference is that 'a number of its citizens returned to Judah after the Exile (Ezra ii. 21)'; the town was probably an insignificant village and is not mentioned in the Books of Maccabees or (as a contemporary place) by Josephus. Presence of a small Judean community from the return (c. 538 BCE; c.).

Estimate by Stephen Pfann and Fr. Jerome Murphy-O'Connor (reported by AP, Karin Laub, Dec. 1994): 'Bethlehem was a typical Jewish village at the time of Jesus' birth, with a population of 2,000 to 3,000 people'; people lived in clans in one- or two-room houses built around caves. Midpoint of range 2000-3000 used; total population of a village the source describes as Jewish. Year: time of Jesus' birth, late reign of Herod, c. 6-4 BCE (c.). Method of derivation not stated in the report.

William F. Albright (as cited by Aleteia, 2017) estimated the population of Bethlehem at the time of Jesus' birth at about 300 people, implying only six or seven male children aged two or under; other scholars put the number of such children at 10-20 in Bethlehem and its surroundings. Population left blank because this source does not state the town's Jewish/Judean character (brief rule on total-population estimates); Albright's original publication not checked. Year c. 6-4 BCE (c.).

Matthew 2:1, 5-6: 'In the time of King Herod, after Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea'; the chief priests and scribes cite Micah ('Bethlehem, in the land of Judah'). Literary attestation of a Judean settlement at Bethlehem under Herod (c. 6-4 BCE; c.; Gospel written late 1st c. CE). No count.

Matthew 2:16 (event): Herod 'sent and killed all the children in and around Bethlehem who were two years old or under' (Massacre of the Innocents, c. 4 BCE, before Herod's death; c.). Historicity disputed by modern scholars; no number given in the text (later liturgical figure of 14,000 is legendary). Population blank; a casualty event, not a population count.

Biblical Archaeology Society, 'Not So Little Town of Bethlehem' (abstract/introduction only): against the traditional view of a quiet pastoral hamlet, 'there may be reason to believe that it was actually a vibrant urban center during the Second Temple period'; clue: 'the Lower Aqueduct, part of a major building project that conducted water directly through the heart of Bethlehem' (aqueduct dated Hasmonean/Herodian). Year = early Roman period midpoint (63 BCE-70 CE = 4). Suggests a sizeable settlement; no figure.

CONTRARY VIEW, not evidence of presence: archaeologist Aviram Oshri (IAA), quoted by Al Jazeera (2004), states that several major excavations in Bethlehem near Jerusalem found 'no evidence ... of habitation at the time of Jesus'; 'All the remains were from many centuries earlier or several centuries later'. Population left blank (absence of evidence is not documented absence; not 0). Year = early Roman period midpoint (4).

Luke 2:1-4: during the registration 'taken while Quirinius was governor of Syria' (6 CE; Luke's dating, which conflicts with Matthew's Herodian date), Joseph went 'to Judea, to the city of David called Bethlehem, because he was descended from the house and family of David'. Literary attestation of Bethlehem as a Judean town with Davidic family connections. No count.

John 7:42: Jerusalem crowd asks whether the Messiah 'comes from Bethlehem, the village where David lived'. Describes Bethlehem as a village (kome) in Jesus' time (c. 30 CE; c.; Gospel written c. 90-100 CE), suggesting a small community. No count.

Encyclopaedia Judaica via Jewish Virtual Library: 'Jews inhabited the city until the time of Bar Kokhba'; in 135 CE a Roman garrison was stationed there to root out remnants of Bar Kokhba's army, and later a gentile population lived there and built a temple to Adonis (Jerome, Ep. 58). Continuous Jewish habitation through the end of the Second Temple period (row placed at 70 CE); the post-135 events fall outside the period. No count.
